newsitem.title: USA: Fed's Broaddus--U.S. economic risks tilted upward.
newsitem.headline: Fed's Broaddus--U.S. economic risks tilted upward.

text.p: RICHMOND, Va. - The potential exists for both below-average economic growth and faster-than-expected activity as 1997 gets underway, but overall the risks are tilted slightly to the upside, Federal Reserve Bank of Richmond President Alfred Broaddus said on Wednesday.

"There are risks in the outlook both on the upside and downside," Broaddus said in a speech to the Richmond Society of Financial Analysts. "My own view ... is that they are tilted, at least a little bit, to the upside."

Broaddus pointed out that the consensus of most economists' forecasts calls for trend growth of around 2 to 2-1/4 percent with inflation holding near 3 percent or perhaps a little bit below. He called that a "reasonable" projection.
Concerning the upside risks, however, he said the high level of activity in the economy could mean a risk of inflation.
"An upside risk with respect to growth probably means an upside risk with respect to inflation because the economy is currently operating at a very high level," Broaddus said.
"You see that in a number of sectors, especially the labor market. Labor markets are really exceptionally tight," he added.

Discussing the economy at the close of 1996, Broaddus described the recent data as "quite strong," and he speculated that many of the forecasts for gross domestic product growth would veer toward the upper end of the range of the 2.5 to 3 percent rate.
Turning to the subject of monetary policy, Broaddus said that accepting an inflation rate of 3 percent as a "permanent condition" was not a credible long-term strategy.
Instead, he said full price-level stability should be the Fed's overriding objective.
"That does not mean that we should shoot for a zero (Consumer Price Index) every month," he said.

"But in my view it does mean taking actions and making sure that we will gradually reduce the CPI from its current rate of around three percent over a multi-year timeframe down closer to two percent and then holding it there for the long run," he added.
Asked in the question-and-answer session about proposals to invest some Social Security money in the stock market, Broaddus said the idea was not a panacea for the problems facing the program.
